data.title: Market sell-off, tax scrutiny and growth: key figures shaping investor sentimentA stock market slump, Beijing’s tax enforcement drive and fresh GDP data are among the developments drawing investors’ a
data.description:
As regional equities tumbled and hopes for investor stimulus faded, the Hang Seng Index fell to a seven-month low. Attention also remained focused on Beijing’s intensified scrutiny of offshore wealth and tax compliance. Macroeconomic data pointed to steady, if uneven, domestic momentum.
Here are the core figures capturing market attention this week.
Hong Kong stocks suffer steepest drop in 7 months
The Hang Seng Index sank 3.03 per cent in a single session to 22,934.68 points, its worst performance since March, as slowing profit growth among major tech firms and reduced expectations for stimulus weighed on sentiment.
Investors were also concerned about potential share sales ahead of Beijing’s Thursday deadline for offshore trust gains. Shares of Chinese toymaker Bloks Group plunged after its chairman sold a 1.6 per cent stake for HK$250 million (US$31.9 million), a move that some market watchers linked to liquidity needs arising from the new tax regime.
China’s tax workforce recruitment drive accelerates
China’s 2027 national civil service recruitment plan includes 24,013 tax-related positions, accounting for more than 67 per cent of all vacancies, up from over 65 per cent a year earlier.
The expansion of the tax workforce is drawing attention from businesses and wealthy families as compliance climbs higher on the policy agenda and authorities intensify enforcement efforts.
Treasury yields slip below 5 per cent threshold
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note dropped below 5 per cent on Thursday for the first time in a month. The benchmark fell as low as 4.95 per cent in intraday trading, while yields on 30-year and five-year bonds also declined.
China’s economy grows 4.6 per cent
China’s economy expanded 4.6 per cent year on year in the first three quarters, meeting the lower end of official full-year targets while highlighting a persistent divide between strong exports and weak domestic demand.
Hong Kong secures strategic investment pledges
Hong Kong on Thursday attracted its seventh batch of 18 strategic enterprises, including Solana and Johnson & Johnson, which pledged more than HK$10 billion in investment and 1,600 high-end jobs to bolster the city’s tech and financial sectors.
US banks pile into dim sum bonds
According to a Bank of America report, US lenders helped drive a 68 per cent surge in issuance of offshore yuan-denominated bonds – known as dim sum bonds – lifting total fundraising to 774 billion yuan (US$116 billion). The surge comes as Wall Street increasingly taps Chinese capital markets even as the yield premium over dollar funding continues to narrow.

data.title: How Operation Santa Claus grew from Christmas donations to ‘engine’ of change
data.description:
Over nearly four decades, Operation Santa Claus (OSC) has grown from a quirky holiday fundraiser into an “engine” for community change in Hong Kong.
For some beneficiaries, the journey was a full circle. Rachel Chow Chiu-yan learned about the fundraising drive in Young Post when she was a student, later pitched for funds on behalf of a group helping teenage girls and later joined the charity.
“Ten to 20 years ago, Operation Santa Claus disbursed some funding to charities that saw it as seed money. Now, after successful pilot schemes, the initiatives have been replicated,” Chow, former senior manager of the programme, said.
The drive was established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988.
But the drive was preceded by early fundraising campaigns from the public broadcaster in the 1960s that featured quirky stunts to attract donations.
Tony Baynes, former head of Radio 3 at RTHK and a co-founder of OSC, recalled that Captain Hamish McNinch of the British Army Air Corps dropped from a helicopter onto a Star Ferry building dressed as Santa Claus in 1981.
“Santa stepped out onto ... [the] Star Ferry building on the Hong Kong side and came down to meet a horde of children who’d gathered especially for the occasion,” Baynes said.

Funds raised from the event went to the Duchess of Kent Children’s Hospital at Sandy Bay.
Since its inception in 1988, OSC has raised more than HK$415 million, supporting 382 charitable projects and helping over 100,000 people.
Each year, OSC identifies several themes and chooses NGOs to fund while connecting corporate donors with the organisations.
Recent fundraising activities included rooftop farming, corporate volunteers making mochi alongside children with special needs and a charity “hash” run mixing exercise and treasure hunting in Santa Claus costumes.
This year, the scheme will support groups tackling poverty, improving health and well-being and promoting inclusivity.
Chow recalled making her pitch for an NGO to OSC.
“[OSC was] really concerned during the pitching process as to whether I could share human stories [of beneficiaries] with the selection panel,” she said.
“Because of this, when I arrived here as a staff member, I also placed much emphasis on this aspect. This is because this is one of the niches in OSC’s charity legacy too.”

She also explained how the drive had evolved over the years, saying: “To me, OSC is like a citywide engine to unlock a spirit of giving across the city. Like an engine, it will keep on moving and keep on unlocking everyone’s generosity.”
Some past recipients had also become partners of the scheme, she noted.
Among them is Pia Wong, founder and CEO of NGO consultancy Purpose Impact Action.
She first worked with OSC as a beneficiary in 2014 when she was an executive director at Bring Me A Book Hong Kong, which promotes literacy. She later returned as a strategic impact partner to help OSC develop a new framework to evaluate the effects of the philanthropy.

Wong said she hoped to turn the long list of beneficiaries into a community that could pool their insights and help each other.
She is developing a “theory of change” model for OSC, where goals are mapped out to reverse-engineer step-by-step outcomes needed to achieve the aims.
Wong said the model would lead to a better understanding of NGOs’ needs and how OSC could support them.
“Back in 2014 it was very much “we’re kind of helping as a funder and you were the beneficiary”, whereas now it is “let’s see how we can work together’,” she said.

data.title: Halloween comes early to Hong Kong as festivities draw crowds, lift bar business
data.description:
Halloween has arrived early in Hong Kong, with costumed revellers and families thronging the city’s streets a week early and some establishments seeing business increase by up to 20 per cent.
The streets of Central were packed on Saturday as visitors and locals alike joined events held under the Tourism Board’s inaugural “Hong Kong Halloween Month”.
The campaign, which started last Saturday, involves street celebrations in Central, including Lan Kwai Fong, Kai Tak, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui East on three consecutive Saturdays, culminating on Halloween night.
Hundreds of people of all ages filled Chater Road as part of “Halloween in Central”, which featured a large eyeball installation at Statue Square, as well as ghoulish face painting and themed food and drink options, including cake pops shaped like eyeballs.
Among those taking part in the celebrations was 40-year-old Hongkonger Stephen Poon, whose daughters Gisele, five, and Gabryel, three, were dressed as Slinky from Pixar’s Toy Story films.
“I think they are doing a really good job,” Poon, who works in accounting, said of the Tourism Board’s event.
He said there had not been much for families to do in the city since the Covid-19 pandemic, and was glad he could bring his daughters out for some family fun.
Poon added that the event had “definitely increased” his spending, with the family planning to buy about HK$500 (US$64) worth of food and other items throughout the day.
“It’s just such a vibe,” he said.

Phil Murphy, founder and managing director of Pyjama, the firm in charge of food and drink at the event, said that given it was the first year, he would be happy just to break even.
Nonetheless, he said business seemed to be “doing quite well” given the foot traffic in the area.
“I think next weekend is going to be brilliant,” he said. “This is the practice run.”
Nearby, Lan Kwai Fong was also bustling as the sun set on Saturday, with dozens of costumed revellers enjoying themselves in the popular nightlife district.
By 9pm, the district was packed with thousands of people slowly snaking their way through its streets, while a Halloween-themed DJ performance across Victoria Harbour in East Tsim Sha Tsui also drew large crowds.
Allan Zeman, chairman of Lan Kwai Fong Group, said business at some of the bars in the area was up by 10 to 20 per cent so far this month.
“Last Saturday was crazy,” he said. “There were so many people, people dancing in costumes.
“Tonight will be similar – really, really busy. The whole city has really come alive this Halloween.”
He added that Halloween created a “really great atmosphere” in the city and also attracted many visitors from mainland China.
The month-long campaign forms part of a tourism strategy outlined in February’s budget to place greater emphasis on festivals that are less prominent on the mainland, including Halloween, to draw more visitors to the city.
Kiki Weng Qi, a 21-year-old university student visiting from Shenzhen, was among the mainland visitors in the area on Saturday night.
While Weng, who was dressed as video game character Mario, said she had visited Hong Kong before, she was marking her first Halloween there with her friend, 19-year-old Xie Man Si, who was dressed as a pumpkin.
“The Halloween celebrations in Hong Kong are particularly great,” she said. “There are similar activities in Shenzhen but there are not so many people.”
The day trippers said they planned to spend HK$2,000 between them on souvenirs and other shopping before returning to Shenzhen later on Saturday.
Despite the early celebrations, some bars in the area were still taking a cautious approach to the festivities.
Many people passing through Lan Kwai Fong were keen to just walk around and take photos of the Halloween decorations, rather than stop for a drink.
“We don’t have a crystal ball,” said a bar employee who declined to be named. “Of course, we want it to be busier than last year. If sales are as good as last year, it will be considered a good thing.”

data.title: 33 held in crackdown on credit card theft ring targeting Hongkongers in Shenzhen
data.description:
Hong Kong and mainland Chinese police have arrested 33 people in a joint operation to crack down on a suspected credit card theft syndicate targeting city residents who travel across the border for leisure, with losses exceeding HK$1.8 million (US$229,500).
Superintendent Tsang Chun-kit of police’s crime Kowloon East Regional Headquarters said the syndicate had allegedly stolen Hongkongers’ credit cards in Shenzhen, and then immediately brought those cards back to the city to make purchases for resale as profit.
“All victims had been to tourist hotspots in Shenzhen for leisure before the crime happened. They didn’t check their personal belongings after the trip until banks notified them of abnormally large transaction records,” Tsang said.
The superintendent added that the Kowloon East regional technology and financial crime unit had exchanged intelligence with Shenzhen’s public security bureau and conducted an in-depth investigation before the agencies took separate enforcement action.
Hong Kong police had arrested 11 men and five women, aged between 17 and 45, in the city for the operation on suspicion of handling stolen goods, conspiracy to defraud and obtaining property by deception.
Those arrested locally included two core members of the syndicate, 13 runners known as “card carriers” and one employee of a second-hand electronic device shop. They were suspected of being involved in at least 60 reports involving stolen credit cards and losses over HK$1.8 million.
The single case with the highest loss involved HK$110,000.
Mainland authorities arrested 11 men and six women, aged between 36 and 56, in Shenzhen for the operation. They were arrested for suspected theft and handling or hiding criminal proceeds.
Chief Inspector Fung Chi-tat of the regional technology and financial crime unit headquarters of Kowloon East said the syndicate was highly organised with a three-tier structure.
The first layer of the syndicate’s operations involved hiring thieves and “card carriers”.
“They would use guest houses near border checkpoints in Shenzhen as a gathering spot for ‘card carriers’,” Fung said.
With runners in place, the syndicate would then arrange for supervisors, who would monitor the handover of stolen credit cards from the thieves to the “card carriers”. These supervisors would also travel between Hong Kong and the mainland to deliver stolen credit cards to “card carriers” and monitor their purchases.
The final layer of the syndicate’s modus operandi involved “card carriers” buying expensive mobile phones for resale to obtain cash. Fung added that the syndicate’s “card carriers” had also been instructed to sell mobile phones at a designated second-hand electronic device shop.
Senior Inspector Chow Ka-yun from the regional technology and financial crime unit of Kowloon East said city officers had been arresting suspected syndicate members between August and October.
Arrest operations included police intercepting suspected syndicate members outside MTR stations where supervised deliveries of stolen credit cards took place, shops where “card carriers” attempted to make purchases and the designated second-hand electronic device shop where “card carriers” sold the mobile phones they bought.
Hong Kong officers also confiscated 13 phones bought with the stolen credit cards, nine stolen cards and multiple receipts of relevant purchases.

data.title: Hong Kong must revive growth and drive reforms with government’s ‘visible hand’
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities should act as a “visible hand” to break down barriers erected by vested interests and revive growth momentum through reform under its maiden five-year plan, a former Beijing official overseeing the city’s affairs has said.
Deng Zhonghua, former deputy director of the State Council’s Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, also said on Saturday that Hong Kong had to empower emerging industries through deregulation and improve mechanisms for sharing the benefits of development in housing, healthcare, elderly care and education.
Deng said the city’s five-year blueprint would address “deep-rooted conflicts” in Hong Kong, including entrenched vested interests and uneven benefits from development, through a reform-oriented approach.
“[The five-year plan] shifted from a free market adopting a positive non-interventionist approach to an organic combination of an efficient market and a capable government,” said Deng, who is now president of the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank.
“[This entails] performing the role of the ‘visible hand’ of the government to effectively regulate and guide in areas where the market fails and reinforce the leading role.”
Speaking at a seminar in Shenzhen, titled “Five-year plans of Hong Kong and Macau and their integration into and service to the overall national development”, Deng described Hong Kong’s five-year plan as a milestone in the implementation of the “one country, two systems” principle, which fully aligned with the national blueprint.
Pointing to long-standing challenges in Hong Kong and Macau, including a narrow economic structure, insufficient growth momentum, entrenched vested interests and uneven distribution of development benefits among residents, Deng said the five-year plans of both cities sought to tackle these issues through reform. Macau released its third five-year plan in August.
“The key to overcoming these challenges lies in breaking down blockades of vested interests, fostering and expanding new growth drivers and new tracks,” Deng said.
“We can only achieve breakthroughs in economic and social development and break down blockades of vested interests through reform. We can only generate new growth momentum and unleash the vitality through innovation.”

Highlighting reform measures in Hong Kong’s five-year plan, including developing an international innovation and technology centre and a high-calibre talent hub, Deng urged the government to maintain a reform mindset throughout implementation, particularly in supporting emerging industries and improving residents’ livelihoods.
“The implementation of the five-year plan relies on innovation,” he said. “It is not only about implementing the reform and innovative measures well, but also about further breaking free from fixed mindsets and path dependence in actual work.”
Deng urged officials to pursue institutional innovation to deregulate and empower the development of emerging industries, establish a fault-tolerant and error-correction mechanism with bold reform and innovation within the legal framework.
He also called for improving mechanisms for sharing the fruits of development in livelihood areas such as housing, healthcare, elderly care and education.
Deng also said the five-year plan marked a shift in Hong Kong’s approach to governance and would improve its effectiveness, but it had to be upheld to turn the blueprint into practice.
He noted that the blueprints enabled Hong Kong and Macau to shift from passive responses and short-term measures to proactive, comprehensive and long-term planning for future development.
They preserved core advantages such as free-port status, low tax rates, marketisation and the rule of law, while strengthening development guidance through policy incentives and government funding, Deng added.
Wang Zhenmin, dean of the Institute for Governance Studies at Tsinghua University, also stressed at the seminar that Hong Kong’s five-year plan aimed to tackle deep-rooted problems the market economy had failed to resolve, particularly the wealth gap and a narrow economic structure.
He rejected criticism that the document would turn the city into a mainland China-style socialist system.
Noting that 1.65 million Hongkongers were in poverty in 2020 and that many families still lived in notorious subdivided flats, Wang said fundamental problems remained unresolved despite some improvement. He added that the five-year plan sought to guide market forces to address these “pain points”.
“Relying solely on the market will only intensify the conflicts and aggravate the situation. This is Hong Kong’s greatest shortcoming,” Wang said.
“If this shortcoming is not addressed, not only will economic and social development be difficult to sustain, but it will also be hard to maintain social stability.”
At the same event, Gao Xiang, president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a prominent Beijing-based state research institute and think tank, said the five-year blueprint served as a key instrument of executive-led governance.
He noted that Hong Kong’s five-year plan set out more than 100 indicators that would allow the outcomes of governance to be examined.
“Under the framework of the five-year plan, executive-led governance becomes an operable, verifiable and accountable institutional arrangement,” Gao added.
Tam Yiu-chung, formerly the city’s sole member of Beijing’s top legislative body, proposed establishing a third-party assessment mechanism to enable independent and continuous monitoring of the plan’s implementation.
He suggested the academy could lead, working with local academic institutions and think tanks, to support midterm adjustments to the blueprint.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu had earlier played down the idea, saying Hong Kong did not need to follow the mainland practice of commissioning third-party organisations to evaluate policy implementation.
Speaking on the sidelines of the seminar, Italian economist Pompeo Della Posta, a professor at the Belt and Road School of Beijing Normal University, said that some European businesses remained sceptical about the mainland market, and Hong Kong could leverage its financial and legal system to help them mitigate risks.
“Europeans still keep deep in their mind about the appropriateness of the Chinese system and the risks and the dangers,” Posta said.
“Passing through Hong Kong and setting their activities in Hong Kong and establishing contracts and relationships in Hong Kong might induce them to feel a bit safer.”

data.title: Abby Choi trial so far: ex-father-in-law lied to rent village flat, bought mincer
data.description:
The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung rented a village house flat under false pretences and bought a meat mincer and multiple saws as he allegedly prepared for the model’s killing, a court has heard.
More evidence emerged regarding how three of Choi’s former in-laws allegedly planned her murder and the disposal of her body as the High Court trial entered its fourth week.
Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial for allegedly murdering the 28-year-old influencer on February 21, 2023.
The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to the offence before the trial began last month.
Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were discovered at a 600 square foot rental flat on the ground floor of a three-storey house in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village on February 24 that year.
Hui Yan-yan, the landlady at the time, said Kwong Kau told her that he wanted a place to spend time with his wife after retiring. He also allegedly claimed that his son, daughter-in-law and their children were returning from Australia and would be living at his Mong Kok residence.
There was no evidence that either of Kwong’s two sons was living overseas just before their father rented the flat.
Hui said Kwong gave her the contact details of his supposed wife, but she subsequently learned from the news that the woman was his mistress. The presiding judge rejected that part of her evidence as hearsay.
She also noted that Kwong Kau had specifically asked whether there were surveillance cameras installed inside the rental flat when he signed the agreement on February 5, 2023.

Kwong Kau earlier admitted that he visited a kitchenware supplier in Yau Ma Tei and bought a commercial meat mincer, a 14-by-14-inch soup pot, a wooden chopping board and a frying sieve for HK$8,700 (US$1,110) on February 8.
A saleswoman at the shop said he also asked about the price of an industrial-grade bone grinder after buying the mincer, but decided against the purchase upon learning that it cost HK$35,000.
Cho Chin-to, who lived at the flat above at the time of the incident, said the flat’s windows were completely sealed between February 15 and 18, and that people outside the premises could not see what happened inside.
Cho said he noticed the sound of heavy objects being carried into the flat at around 3pm on February 21, before he heard electric saws and noise that appeared to come from renovation work.
He added that a “very nice aroma” resembling a typical radish and carrot soup came out of the ground-floor flat at around 7pm and lingered for a long time that night.

The court heard Choi’s head was found in a large soup pot that also contained pieces of cooked carrot and radish, while her two legs and part of her pelvis and spine were found inside a refrigerator.
Senior government chemist Dr Tam Cheok-ning said he found a cut mark on the spine that was consistent with the blade of one of two electric saws found in the flat.
Tam also opined that the two boxes found inside the premises were the same ones the defendants allegedly used to carry Choi’s body.
Prosecutors said the alleged murder arose from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin.
Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill his former daughter-in-law so that he could keep it for himself.
The trial heard Choi covered the entirety of the flat’s HK$60 million purchase price when Kwong Kau bought the flat on her behalf in 2019.
Property agent Marco Wong Tak-sing said Kwong pocketed HK$6.97 million in cash rebate and paid HK$3.09 million in stamp duty for the purchase, but he was unsure whether he settled the sum using his own money.
Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, previously alleged that the Kwong family had been living off her family’s wealth in the lead-up to her daughter’s killing.
But Choi’s former chauffeur, Chin Kei-shun, said Anthony Kwong appeared to have given HK$600,000 to Choi when she was having financial difficulties in 2022.
Chan Leong-hang, an employee of Aristo Watch & Jewellery in Tsim Sha Tsui, also said Alex Kwong had asked for part of his proceeds from selling luxury watches to the shop to go to his former partner.
Tam, the forensic scientist, is expected to continue his oral testimony when the trial resumes next week.

data.title: 16,000 sign up for exam to drive taxis or ride-hailing cars in Hong Kong
data.description:
About 16,000 Hong Kong residents have signed up for a joint exam to drive taxis or ride-hailing cars, the transport chief has said.
Speaking on a radio programme on Saturday, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the allocation arrangement for the 10,000 ride-hailing vehicle permits would be announced in November, with the government considering increasing the odds for certain drivers in the lottery draw.
“We are pleased to see the enthusiastic response to the joint examination. We’ve been considering how to make the best use of the quota of 10,000 permits to ensure they can be given to those who are genuinely dedicated and capable of providing ride-hailing services,” she said.
“Making early preparations, such as signing up for or completing the examination, reflects their genuine commitment to taking part early in providing point-to-point services … We hope that within the lottery system, these individuals can be given higher odds of being selected.”
The minister said the government was also considering giving higher odds to those who had owned a private vehicle for a certain period, such as a year.
Many young people were providing ride-hailing services as a part-time job and the system would not exclude them, she added.

Hong Kong recently passed legislation to regulate local ride-hailing services, capping the total number of vehicle permits at 10,000.
The new rules require residents to first pass an assessment to apply for either a taxi-driving licence or a ride-hailing permit, while existing cab drivers can apply for the permit directly without taking the test.
Ride-hailing platform operators are also required to obtain dedicated licenses, with applications to close on October 30.
Chan said the pass rate of the exam was more than 60 per cent, which showed that the prospective drivers were taking the test seriously.
She said the government expected to announce the first batch of licensed operators by the end of November at the earliest.
“Through this exercise, we hope to attract capable, experienced platform operators to set up and run their businesses in Hong Kong,” she said.
“Most importantly, they must be committed to establishing a local presence with their own dedicated teams, while aligning with the government’s policy of enabling ride-hailing services and taxis to coexist and complement one another.
“We will also evaluate the passenger experience, such as waiting times and the mechanism of assigning vehicles … to select what best meets the needs of the public, while offering diverse options to foster healthy competition.
Separately, Chan said the Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme, which was launched Friday last week had received 32 registrations so far.
The first batch of five yachts that sailed to Hong Kong on October 16 stayed in the city for three to four days, docking at either yacht clubs or designated government berthing areas, she added.
The five vessels included a superyacht about 100 feet long, Chan said.
The minister said some visitors chose to remain on the yachts, but others stayed in hotels and went ashore to sightsee and shop, visiting Stanley, Central and theme parks.
“I believe the scheme opens up a new travel model for our tourism and retail economy,” she said.
More than 300 mainland Chinese yacht masters had qualified to navigate Hong Kong waters. she noted.
To enable more yacht masters to participate, the Marine Department would commission local training institutions to open online courses, the minister said.

data.title: Hong Kong customs seizes 600 million illicit cigarettes in first 9 months of 2026
data.description:
Hong Kong customs officers seized 600 million illicit cigarette sticks in the first three quarters of this year, the department chief has said as he revealed plans to roll out more advanced contraband detection equipment at additional border checkpoints to ease manpower pressure.
Commissioner of Customs and Excise Chan Tsz-tat told a radio programme on Saturday that the seizure amount in the first nine months this year nearly matched the 2025 annual total.
He said that of the 600 million sticks seized, 200 million were destined for other locations but were intercepted in Hong Kong after customs received intelligence.
“We have around 16,000 cases of illicit cigarette seizures that involved passengers who did not declare they were carrying over 19 sticks of cigarettes,” Chan said.
These cases are among the 18,000 illicit cigarette cases customs detected from January to September this year.
No serious drug cases were intercepted at the revamped Huanggang Port since it began operations last Monday, the commissioner added.
When asked whether customs operations at the revamped Huanggang Port were smooth following long queues amid crowd surges over the Chung Yeung Festival weekend, the customs chief said both passenger and cargo clearance were steady.
“The bottleneck was not at customs checks. Customs clearance hall operations were quite smooth,” Chan said.
At the revamped Huanggang Port, vehicle clearance is handled through a “joint one-stop” clearance lane. Drivers first pass through a customs front kiosk before sharing their identity and biometric data at a machine that shares data with five government departments, including customs, across Hong Kong and Shenzhen for the driver’s clearance.
Should customs checks be deemed necessary, drivers would be notified at the customs front kiosk to drive to a separate clearance hall for checks.

To cope with increased manpower demand for the revamped Huanggang Port, the department has reassigned staff from other border checkpoints, cancelled staff members’ leave and hired a small number of retired staff to help man the newly opened land boundary checkpoint.
“As more people cross the border, our workload will only increase. Adding manpower may not be the only way to cope,” Chan said.
The customs chief said the department would turn to technology to introduce more advanced equipment to alleviate manpower pressure.
This would include introducing the active millimetre wave detector, a device to scan for contraband items hidden on a person’s body, at more land checkpoints in the future.
The detector uses a wave that is not invasive to the body and may reduce the need for body searches on passengers, according to Chan.
With the unprecedented joint clearance system, officials earlier said processing time at the revamped Huanggang crossing could be cut to five minutes from about 30 minutes.
Hong Kong residents who hold a valid mainland Chinese travel permit can use their Hong Kong ID cards interchangeably at the joint clearance channel for both outbound and inbound trips.
The crossing is expected to be able to handle up to 300,000 travellers a day. The Immigration Department said it expected about 100,000 people to use Huanggang Port daily during initial operations. It can also handle 15,000 vehicles a day.

data.title: Crypto platform on alert lists opens Hong Kong office, prompting calls for scrutiny
data.description:
A cryptocurrency trading platform on Hong Kong and Canadian regulators’ alert lists has opened an office in the city, prompting experts to urge closer scrutiny of how such firms promote themselves without undermining an open business environment.
Experts told the South China Morning Post that inclusion on a regulator’s alert list did not necessarily mean a company had broken the law. But they urged authorities to step up oversight of how such firms marketed regulated financial products.
Polar Tensor, a cryptocurrency investment platform that said it held company registrations in seven jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, Panama and the US states of Montana and Wyoming, opened an office at One Hysan Avenue in Causeway Bay in August.
A source told the SCMP that the platform was being monitored by authorities.
The firm has been on the alert list of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) since early August. It also appears on investment caution lists issued by regulators in the Canadian provinces of British Columbia, Quebec and Alberta.
The SFC has classified Polar Tensor as a suspicious virtual asset trading platform, saying the firm and its associated websites were not licensed to conduct regulated activities in the city.
An SFC spokesman declined to comment beyond the information published on the regulator’s website.
The regulator said on its website that its alert list included entities that were unlicensed in Hong Kong and believed to be targeting local investors or claiming an association with the city.
Hong Kong has a licensing regime for stablecoins, a type of cryptocurrency pegged to assets such as the United States dollar. Investing through a cryptocurrency platform that is not licensed in the city is not itself illegal.
However, it is illegal to offer unlicensed stablecoins to retail investors in Hong Kong or actively market them to the public.

The SCMP visited Polar Tensor’s office twice in August, including for its opening event, and spoke to people who said they worked with the organisation.
Posts on Polar Tensor’s Telegram channel showed that the platform organised three days of events in Hong Kong in August. These included a seminar and gala dinner at a five-star hotel, followed by an office opening party, another dinner and a junk party.
At the office opening, a staff member said the premises were for “appointments” but declined to explain what these involved.
He described those attending as “members” of the platform rather than clients.
The office was sparsely furnished, with rows of tables set up for the opening party. It was closed when the SCMP visited again later in August.
Polar Tensor describes itself on its website as an “advanced AI-powered trading platform”.
Documents seen by the SCMP showed that a German citizen established a company called Polar Tensor LAB in Hong Kong last year, with a registered address in Sheung Wan.
During the SCMP’s visit to Polar Tensor’s Causeway Bay office in October, the doors were locked with no one answering.
A security guard at One Hysan Avenue said that she had not seen anyone at the office for the past two months.
Polar Tensor’s registered entity in Hong Kong remains active as of October, the SCMP has learned.
Lawmaker Johnny Ng Kit-chong said inclusion on a regulator’s alert list did not mean a platform had broken the law.
But he urged authorities to do more to develop regulations governing how firms selling regulated financial products, such as cryptocurrencies, could promote themselves.
“Setting up an office in Hong Kong itself does not offend the law, but opening an office in Hong Kong to sell these products, they would need to register with the Securities and Futures Commission,” he said.

Ng, who is also a technology entrepreneur, urged law enforcement agencies to go beyond issuing alerts about suspicious platforms and firms. He also called on authorities to consider whether social media platforms should bear some responsibility for the content promoted on their services.
Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung said inclusion on an alert list was not in itself grounds for arrest, but suspicions about a platform’s operations or business should prompt proactive investigations.
Li, who is also an investor, said common legal violations involving firms offering unlicensed financial products included actively promoting them to the public or soliciting money from users.
But he said public promotion could be difficult to define, as organisations holding invitation-only events could argue they were not promoting themselves to the wider public.
Acknowledging the difficulty of balancing an open business environment with crime prevention, Li said authorities could strengthen due diligence to prevent suspicious businesses from gaining access to the public or appearing to have official endorsement.
“For example, I think rentals of major convention venues or advertisements in MTR stations need to be checked,” he said.
Responding to a SCMP inquiry, a police spokesman said the force had received no reports concerning Polar Tensor.
“If we discover criminal elements, we will follow up solemnly and in accordance with the law,” he said.

data.title: Private secondary sector expands as Hong Kong universities’ reputation grows
data.description:
The number of private secondary schools in Hong Kong has risen by more than half in five years as demand for alternative curricula grows and new operators seek to attract families drawn by the city’s highly ranked universities, education authorities and principals have said.
Between 2021-22 and 2025-26, the number of private secondary institutions increased from 16 to 25, a jump of 56.3 per cent, Education Bureau figures show.
Leaders at schools offering alternative curriculum pathways said that more mainland Chinese and overseas students were considering Hong Kong universities due to the institutions’ rising global reputation amid geopolitical concerns.
Over the same period, the number of private primary schools also rose from 62 to 65, up 4.8 per cent.
Private schools offering a non-local curriculum, which charge between HK$100,000 and HK$300,000 (US$12,800 and US$38,260) a year in tuition fees, do not receive government land grants and have no caps on their ratio of local to non-local students.
International schools, however, typically operate under fixed ratios of non-local students, while private independent schools, which receive government land grants, must enrol at least 70 per cent local pupils.
The Education Bureau pointed to a stronger economy and shifting parental preferences as factors behind the rising number of private schools.
“Driven by overall economic growth and a growing demand for diverse educational choices that cater to varying parental preferences for education, the sectors of international schools and other private schools offering a formal curriculum have been steadily expanding,” it said.
St Bees (Anchors) Sixth Form College is one new private school entering the sector. It is set to open in West Kowloon’s Coronation Circle for the 2027–28 academic year.
David Cardwell, founding co-chair of St Bees and former pro-vice-chancellor at the University of Cambridge, said Hong Kong’s established international curricula give families diverse pathways to maximise their children’s university prospects.
“Hong Kong is the perfect place to study – a city of just 7 million people with five universities in the global top 100. It is unprecedented,” he said.
St Bees will offer A-level and International General Certificate of Secondary Education programmes. Its registration application is being reviewed by the bureau, with fees to be confirmed upon approval.
Cardwell said its graduates were expected to pursue higher education globally, whether at Hong Kong universities, in the United Kingdom or in the United States.
The school is targeting 150 students for its first year of operation, with a long-term capacity of 500.
“We would like to get 30 to 50 per cent international, if possible, but again we do not want to have a cap,” Cardwell added.

School co-chair Danny Wang Tak-chi said it aimed to keep its main cohort local while recruiting internationally, although geopolitical and economic factors would shape its composition in coming years.
Wang said recent adjustments to the visa policy for the dependants of arriving talent – including a two-year residency rule before they could apply for subsidised places at local universities – were designed to ensure recipients contribute to society, not to discourage arrivals.
“The trend of people coming to Hong Kong will just keep growing and growing, as Hong Kong becomes a hub for education in Asia,” he said.
Among the recent graduate cohort at Kellett School, more students, including non-local ones, aspired to enter university in Hong Kong.
The international school said 34 of its 85 graduates this year submitted a total of 112 applications to Hong Kong universities, the most in recent years.
“One of the reasons for the growth in applicants is that five of the world’s top 100 universities are here in Hong Kong, so the city has a very strong reputation for university education,” school principal and CEO Paul Tough said.
“With the government’s intention to develop the university town, the growth is only going to get stronger.”
He added the soaring costs of university education in the US and the UK, combined with a geopolitical climate that had parents wanting their children closer to home, were driving more families towards Hong Kong institutions.
The school, which was established in 1976, opened its Sixth Form Centre at the Bay Hub, a commercial building in Kowloon Bay in August.
The centre can accommodate 240 students, with 225 currently enrolled. The annual tuition fee for Sixth Form is HK$279,100.
As an international school offering the A-level curriculum, Kellett maintains a 70:30 ratio of non-local to local students.

data.title: URA tells owners to avoid hiring lift company at centre of fire safety probe
data.description:
Hong Kong’s Urban Renewal Authority has advised property owners under a subsidy scheme against hiring a contractor that failed to install fire safety components in lifts at hundreds of buildings, saying it had “lost confidence” in the company.
The move came a day after the government suspended the performance rating for Taizoom Elevator, which was found to have failed to install required fire-resistant door frame components at 338 buildings as inspections of its work across the city are carried out.
Industry professionals have urged the government to step up routine inspections of lifts and called on authorities to assist the management of buildings that had signed contracts with the company and had been waiting for work to begin.
“In view of the serious failures involved when Taizoom Elevator replaced lifts for multiple housing estates and buildings, the Urban Renewal Authority (URA) has lost confidence in its services,” a spokesman said in a reply to the South China Morning Post on Friday.
“Therefore [the URA] does not recommend that property owners select Taizoom as the engineering contractor for the Lift Modernisation Subsidy Scheme.”

The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department launched its inspections on October 15 after it was discovered the contractor had installed fire-resistant doors without the required frame components at two estates.
The components prevent flames and smoke from entering the lift shaft in the event of a fire.
The department has also ordered lift companies to check their installations going back a decade and submit reports.
The department said on Thursday that it had suspended the regular rating of the company’s performance due to “serious failures” of its lift installation works.
Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan called on the government to set up a statutory body to oversee building repairs and step up routine inspections.
“The authority could act as an independent third party to monitor building maintenance and conduct spot checks to assist property owners,” Fong said.
Former lawmaker Doreen Kong Yuk-foon, a lawyer by training, said in a social media post on Thursday that she had noted concerns from property owners who had signed contracts with Taizoom but were still waiting for the work to begin.
Kong added that owners had lost confidence in the company and were questioning whether the URA and authorities would offer help.
Police arrested a Taizoom director and two registered lift engineers last Friday, a source said.
Hong Kong had 73,393 lifts as of February, according to official information.

data.title: Jensen Huang pushes AI in energy-rich Kazakhstan, shrugs off bubble fears
data.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is pitching the concept of “sovereign AI” in Kazakhstan – part of his global crusade urging nations to build domestic computing infrastructure using the firm’s chips – as the energy-rich nation emerges as a US-China battleground for artificial intelligence.
Speaking at a fireside chat in Astana on Friday with Kazakh AI and digital development minister Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang said AI was reshaping every industry in a transformation that “affects every single person and country”.
Huang added that Nvidia provided the computing foundation powering AI hubs, which required vast resources, particularly electricity and data.
His remarks come as Kazakhstan seeks to leverage its vast energy reserves to become a regional computing hub by building what Huang calls “AI factories”.
The country holds an estimated 25.6 billion tonnes of coal reserves – among the world’s largest – according to the US Energy Information Administration.
“Because you have so much energy, instead of just exporting energy in the future, you can transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said.
In June, Kazakhstan announced a US$10 billion plan involving Nvidia and American AI infrastructure developer Firebird to build a computing hub in Ekibastuz, a major coal-mining and power-generation centre.
The project envisages deploying around 100,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), with total power capacity reaching up to 1 gigawatt. Its initial 50-megawatt facility is scheduled to open in June next year, with Madiyev estimating the hub could eventually generate at least US$3 billion in annual computing export revenue.
Still, the region’s ambitions face steep structural obstacles.
The Washington-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace warned in April that Central Asia’s digital push could be constrained by unreliable power grids, limited international connectivity and regulatory barriers.

Huang, Nvidia’s 63-year-old founder, has spent much of the past year travelling globally as one of AI’s most prominent evangelists. From Europe to Asia, he has urged governments to build sovereign AI infrastructure – using Nvidia’s coveted chips – to keep control over their own data and cultural capabilities.
Just two days before his Astana appearance, Huang pressed European nations to build out their domestic AI infrastructure during Nvidia’s GPU Technology Conference in Berlin, where the firm unveiled new modular data-centre technology.
However, Huang’s globe-trotting promotional campaign comes amid mounting scepticism over the financial sustainability of the global AI buildout.
Ken Griffin, the billionaire founder of hedge fund Citadel, warned on Wednesday that the AI sector was “almost certainly” in a bubble, raising concerns that an eventual oversupply of computing hardware could drive down prices and undermine the financial returns of megaprojects.
His comments echoed earlier warnings from Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who described the frenzy as a “classic bubble” nearing a potential peak, as well as the Bank of England, which cautioned last month that mounting debt tied to AI infrastructure could amplify losses if profitability expectations faltered.
Huang has brushed off bubble concerns, telling US broadcaster CNBC on Thursday that demand for specialist AI cloud providers remained “off the charts”. Instead, he argued that growth was being bottlenecked by a shortage of working capital across the sector.
“What’s missing … is the working capital to fuel that growth, because there are so many demands across so many sectors of AI,” Huang said.
Kazakhstan’s push into AI also highlights Central Asia’s growing weight in the technology rivalry between Washington and Beijing.
Sharing a roughly 1,700km (1,050-mile) border with China, Kazakhstan has played both sides of the divide. In June, Astana joined Pax Silica – a US-led initiative aimed at securing AI supply chains, energy, chips and data centres – before signing on as a founding member of the China-backed World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation the following month.
Meanwhile, Chinese tech companies have expanded their own presence across Central Asia, pursuing telecommunications, cloud infrastructure and AI model partnerships in Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.

data.title: Hong Kong Legco to review tighter rules on access to land records amid concerns
data.description:
Hong Kong’s legislature will set up a subcommittee to examine proposed restrictions on access to land records following widespread public concern.
At the Legislative Council’s house committee meeting on Friday, lawmakers endorsed establishing the subcommittee to study proposed requirements and procedures under the Land Titles Regulation.
The move came after some legislators and the Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation – including the Land Titles Regulation covering land record search arrangements – at the Legco for negative vetting.
Under negative vetting, subsidiary legislation is first gazetted and then vetted by lawmakers later.
Most of the provisions, including the tightened search arrangements, are scheduled to take effect in the first half of next year.
On Friday, Legco legal adviser Timothy Tso recommended setting up a subcommittee on subsidiary legislation, noting that his team was still examining the details of the changes.
At least five legislators raised their hands in support, including Election Committee constituency members Rebecca Chan Hoi-yan, Andrew Lam Siu-lo and Thomas So Shiu-tsung, alongside Christine Fong Kwok-shan and Mark Chong Ho-fung.
“I also have concerns over whether referencing specific cases during legislative questioning could inadvertently breach the law [if my team has conducted land searches],” Roundtable lawmaker Chong told the South China Morning Post.
He added that when lawmakers conducted research or gathered real-life cases to address policy issues or assist enforcement – such as targeting public housing tenants who illegally own private property – there were fears of unwittingly crossing legal boundaries.
He noted that while the public previously relied on the media to investigate such matters, uncertainty remained over how individuals or lawmakers should proceed if they performed searches themselves.
He also said that no timeline has been set for when the subcommittee would meet, though the Legco secretariat was expected to issue a notice inviting interested lawmakers to join.

The new search arrangements represent the government’s latest step to tighten public access to information, following similar restrictions imposed on the vehicle and companies registries.
The government has maintained that the city currently does not restrict who can access land records and argued that the new arrangements aim to protect privacy while maintaining system transparency and efficiency.
Under the proposed regime, applicants must select from nine specified purposes to obtain essential property information, such as the names of current and former owners, purchase prices, registration dates, encumbrances, application forms and supporting documents for active entries.
These specific purposes include property valuation, due diligence for transactions, building management, legal proceedings, conducting academic and market research and conducting inspections in the public interest.
Applications filed on public interest grounds will be assessed individually by the registrar, who will consider whether the societal benefit outweighs privacy rights and whether the documents might be misused.
Meanwhile, access to historical records – such as past property transfers or complied building orders – will be restricted to 15 categories of applicants.
While the list does not explicitly include journalists, it permits applications from individuals declaring a public interest purpose, current or former property owners, and professionals.
Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan said she backed forming a subcommittee because many details remained unresolved, adding that the government needed to clarify the criteria and definition used to approve applications.
The Hong Kong Journalists Association previously criticised the proposals, stating that authorities had failed to justify the changes or consult the public, while warning that the restrictions would undermine society’s ability to monitor the property market.
Additional reporting by Ng Kang-chung

data.title: Sauce maker to close after 90 years, making way for Northern Metropolis
data.description:
One of Hong Kong’s last traditional sauce makers is to cease operations, ending its 90-year legacy, after authorities cleared land at its Kwu Tung factory on Friday.
Established in 1936, Kui Lee Sauce and Preserved Fruit confirmed to the South China Morning Post that it would close down once its remaining inventory at its shop in Wan Chai was sold.
“Our factory in Kwu Tung has halted production, and all remaining stock is at our retail shop. We will close permanently after selling through all inventory,” an employee of Kui Lee Sauce told an SCMP reporter, who posed as a customer.
As a time-honoured Hong Kong brand, Kui Lee has been passed down through three generations and is known for being “100 per cent made in Hong Kong”.
Having moved from Kowloon City to Kwu Tung in the 1960s, the factory has insisted on making soy sauce and vinegar using traditional sun-drying methods.
Its soy sauce has long been renowned in Hong Kong and has been exported to other markets in recent years, including Taiwan.
On Friday morning, more than 30 security guards and police officers were deployed to the Kui Lee sauce factory and Tong Kok Village in Kwu Tung to execute eviction notices.
The area is subject to a land resumption operation under the government’s Northern Metropolis megaproject, which aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into a technology hub and serve as an economic engine.
People wearing vests marked “NDA” – short for the New Development Areas under the Northern Metropolis strategy – were seen entering the sauce factory and spoke with the owner in a room for more than 30 minutes.

More than 12 security guards stood outside, while another dozen cordoned off the entrance and locked the steel gate.
Most of the guards left the factory at around 12.10pm after a notice was posted on the gate stating that the site had been taken over by the government. November 6 will be the final date for water and electricity supply and clearing items at the site.
Three security guards still stationed at the entrance were allowing workers temporary access to the factory through the gate.
The factory representatives declined to comment on the clearance.
The Lands Department’s clearance operation faced pushback from villagers on the site, many of whom had lived there for half a century.
A handful of residents were packing up the last of their belongings in homes they had lived in for decades, among them the Chan family.
“After all, we’ve lived here for more than 50 years. I feel reluctant to leave,” said Chan, a retiree in her seventies, standing in front of her house and wiping away tears with a towel. “This is half a century of memories.”
Her son, in his forties and born and raised in the house, was wrapping up a final batch of daily necessities with his wife.
“We were told the exact date of the land clearance not long ago, and our electricity was cut two days ago,” Chan’s daughter-in-law said.
“I was washing clothes when the power went off, and we could only use a flashlight to pack our things at night.”
She added that the water pipes had been destroyed by someone in recent days.
“We used to have a big family living here together for a whole life. Now we’re all separated,” she said.
Nearby, dozens of security guards and lands officials had surrounded another resident’s home and were preparing to lock it up, but a dispute broke out when the owner said they had not finished packing.
Staff prevented people from filming or getting closer to the site, citing “security concerns”.

data.title: Cambricon’s third quarter profit surges 148% amid push to replace Nvidia
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence chip giant Cambricon Technologies reported a 147.7 per cent surge in third-quarter profit on Friday, as the country’s aggressive push to replace Nvidia chips continues to fuel high growth among local chipmakers.
The Shanghai-listed chipmaker generated 1.4 billion yuan (US$210 million) in net profit for the three months ended September 30, up from 566.6 million yuan during the same period last year.
Revenue reached 3.5 billion yuan, an increase of 104.5 per cent from a year ago, according to its stock exchange filing. That was faster than the company’s 75.8 per cent revenue increase seen in the second quarter.
Cambricon attributed the revenue surge to its continuous market expansion and efforts to “facilitate the implementation of AI applications”. This top-line increase directly drove the year-on-year surge in total profit and net profit, the company said in the filing.
Shares of Cambricon closed up 5.5 per cent at 932.2 yuan ahead of the earnings release on Friday.
Earlier this week, Hygon Information Technology, another leading domestic AI chipmaker, posted third-quarter revenue of 5.9 billion yuan, an increase of 45.5 per cent year on year. Its net profit for the quarter surged 37.9 per cent year on year to 1 billion yuan.
The momentum at Cambricon and Hygon builds on Beijing’s initiative to develop a self-sufficient AI computing ecosystem, as the country accelerates the deployment of AI infrastructure powered by home-grown chips.

The two companies – regarded as top-tier players in the domestic AI chip sector – are moving rapidly to fill the market vacuum left by Washington’s export controls that have cut off China’s access to advanced AI accelerators from US chip giants like Nvidia.
Analysts said Cambricon’s earnings outlook depended largely on the commercialisation progress of its latest chips, which was in turn affected by supply chain pressures, especially the shortage of high bandwidth memory chips required for AI data centres.
“Cambricon delivered [its] MLU692 to a major cloud service provider in Q3 for testing, but we expect most revenue to be recognised in Q4,” Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a recent research report. “MLU580 shipments also remain limited as higher high bandwidth memory costs pressure unit economics.”
The MLU692 is part of Cambricon’s MLU690 chip series, also known as Siyuan 690. The series can outperform Nvidia’s H20 by 50 to 150 per cent when measured in “tokens per second”, a metric that essentially counts how many words or other data AI can process and spit out, according to an earlier Morgan Stanley report.
Hygon, meanwhile, faces high expectations for its next-generation central processing unit and its deep computing unit – a type of accelerator card designed specifically for AI.
The company said on Thursday that the progress was “on track” with key metrics such as compute density and interconnect bandwidth set to be upgraded, though mass production timelines remained pending.

data.title: China’s humanoid robots go job hunting in South Korea
data.description:
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.
Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence.
A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year.
“China’s new generation of robot companies has global DNA and naturally looks overseas, and South Korea is one of the most important markets in the Asia-Pacific region,” said Ethan Qi, an associate director covering robotics at Counterpoint Research. The lack of locally built humanoid robots available at scale had created an opening for Chinese suppliers, he added.
Commercial foothold
Representatives of Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue in Seoul, agreed to buy UBTech’s lifelike U1 model after seeing its debut in Shenzhen in June, according to Sean Qin, overseas head of the company’s commercial robots division.
The robot, designed with a female appearance and standing 1.68 metres tall, cost around 170,000 yuan (US$25,000) and was delivered to the park last month, Qin said. UBTech entered the South Korean market as early as 2019 and had since sold more than 10,000 robots to dozens of corporate and government customers, he added.
In July, UBTech, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, also announced plans to trial humanoid robots on a South Korean automotive parts production line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker Ajin Industrial. Several UBTech models were undergoing on-site operational tests in the country, Qin said, without providing details.
“As a manufacturing powerhouse, South Korea already makes extensive use of robotic arms, autonomous mobile robots and other conventional systems,” he said. “The next step is to help workers become more productive in tasks that demand greater flexibility. That makes Korea a key market for UBTech and for humanoids more broadly.”
Zhang Yufeng, founder and CEO of Anyverse Dynamics, who previously worked with SK Telecom and Hyundai Motor, said South Korea was “one of our most important overseas markets”.
The Beijing-based start-up teamed up with South Korean coffee chain Hollys at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August to test robots that serve drinks, clear tables and reset seats. The robots were currently undergoing trial operations at a cafe in Beijing, Zhang said.

South Korea ranked as China’s third-largest export market by value for “intelligent bionic robots” in the first nine months of 2026, behind the United States and Japan, according to Chinese customs data. Exports to South Korea totalled US$19.99 million, or 9.7 per cent of the US$206.95 million China shipped globally. China exported 16,559 robots to 108 countries and regions under the customs category, introduced this year, which covers humanoids and robot dogs.
Eight of China’s 10 top-selling humanoid robot makers had been testing the waters in South Korea through product certification, trademark filings and sales channels, according to a report by industry research platform Labsdeep that was cited by Electronic Times this month.
“We plan to begin trials in Korean cafes and other commercial service settings in the fourth quarter, before expanding into manufacturing,” Zhang said, noting that the company had been working on product certification for the market.
Seoul’s stringent Korea Certification requirements prompted UBTech to adapt its communications modules and radio frequency settings for local use, Qin said.
Factories as main testing ground
China’s robotics boom has spawned a wave of unicorn firms over the past two years, some of which have already begun shipping products at scale, backed by an extensive supply chain at home. Their push to find commercial applications to justify the investment and hype surrounding humanoid robots coincides with South Korea’s drive to deploy physical AI across its industrial base.
Seoul is prioritising the technology to strengthen manufacturing as its working-age population shrinks and potential economic growth slows. The government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (US$2.3 billion) in physical AI funding for 2027, more than triple this year’s level.
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources’ Manufacturing AI Transformation programme, dubbed M.AX, supports AI adoption and factory trials involving robots, including humanoids, with a target of 500 AI factories by 2030. The ministry has budgeted 1.1 trillion won for AI transformation this year.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said in August that the government would support factories operated by AI and robots, helping South Korea become “a global leader in manufacturing AI transformation by 2030”.
South Korea’s industrial heavyweights are also moving quickly.
LG Electronics is building its Data Factory in Seoul to train robots for industrial and household applications, while testing robots on its own production lines. Samsung Electronics established its Robotics eXperience division in July, targeting manufacturing before expanding into homes and retail. A bipedal robot designed to operate round the clock in manufacturing and logistics could debut at the CES annual consumer electronics trade show in Las Vegas in January 2027, JoongAng Ilbo reported on Tuesday.
Hyundai Motor Group has begun training Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoids at its factory campus in the US state of Georgia, ahead of a planned 2028 deployment in manufacturing. Doosan Robotics has unveiled AI-powered sanding and palletising systems and is developing robot-control software, with support from Nvidia.
South Korea’s start-up ecosystem is also drawing fresh capital. AI and robotics accounted for 45 per cent of third-quarter investments tracked by The VC, a local start-up and venture capital investment database platform. Within physical AI, funding is flowing to robot makers as well as start-ups developing foundational models for robots and supplying training data.
The country offered a broad range of potential deployment sites in carmaking, shipbuilding and semiconductor manufacturing, Counterpoint’s Qi said. But gaining access was difficult for Chinese suppliers because they needed local customers willing to participate in proof-of-concept trials.
Partners and rivals
The growing presence of Chinese firms has stirred political debate. At a parliamentary audit on October 6, lawmaker Lee Jeong-heon of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea brought robots from China’s Unitree and AgiBot to challenge the government over South Korea’s competitiveness in physical AI.
Lawmaker Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party questioned whether the robots had undergone security checks and accused the National Assembly of providing a stage for Chinese technology.
Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who is also the Science and Information and Communications Technology minister, urged South Korea to ramp up physical AI investment and development, pointing to China’s growing deployment of humanoids.
“China is also deploying more humanoid robots in the field and collecting data,” he said during a Physical AI Tech Week round table in Seoul on October 13, according to news outlet MoneyToday.
Bae questioned whether Korea’s plans were bold enough and called for higher targets to avoid regretting insufficient investment in the future. Companies also needed to shoulder greater responsibility because the government could not support every initiative, he said.
Park Young-hoon, head of the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency’s Shenzhen office, said he also saw room for cooperation.
“Companies need to explore new business opportunities using Shenzhen’s local supply chains and innovation capabilities while competing with Chinese technology companies,” he told local media outlet Newspim in October.
Anyverse Dynamics’ Zhang said he saw the two countries’ industrial strengths as “highly complementary”. South Korea combined global leadership in advanced manufacturing with a capacity for AI innovation, while China offered a comprehensive supply chain, a deep pool of engineering and AI talent, and rapid product iteration, he said.
For UBTech’s Qin, policies favouring domestic companies have not deterred Korean customers from considering Chinese suppliers. “The Korean customers we have dealt with are open to working with Chinese robot makers,” he said.

data.title: Former HSBC insurance veteran joins AIA in latest senior talent move
data.description:
Former HSBC Holdings global insurance head Edward Moncreiffe will join rival AIA Group as regional CEO from November 2, following a path taken by former HSBC Group chairman Mark Tucker, who returned to the Asia-Pacific region’s largest insurer as non-executive chairman last year.
Moncreiffe will oversee AIA’s businesses in India, Sri Lanka, Australia and New Zealand, while serving on the group’s executive committee, according to a company statement issued on Friday. He will report to group CEO and president Lee Yuan Siong.
After 20 years at HSBC, Moncreiffe resigned as global insurance CEO in August. During his tenure, the lender’s insurance business became Hong Kong’s market leader in new life insurance premiums for four consecutive years and sold a record-breaking US$250 million life insurance policy in February 2024.
He is the second high-profile executive to move from HSBC to AIA. Tucker became AIA’s non-executive chairman in October last year after serving as the insurer’s group CEO and president between 2010 and 2017.
The appointment highlights intensifying competition for senior talent in the insurance and wealth management sector in Hong Kong and Asia, as growing numbers of wealthy customers use insurance products for wealth preservation and succession planning.
“I am delighted to be joining AIA, a company distinguished by its exceptional franchise, clear purpose and long-term commitment to Asia,” Moncreiffe said.
“AIA’s businesses in India, Sri Lanka, Australia and New Zealand each have distinct strengths, priorities and opportunities,” he said, adding that he would work with his new team to deliver long-term value for customers, partners and shareholders.
Moncreiffe holds a bachelor’s degree from Durham University and a master of business administration from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. He is also a chartered insurer.
Lee said Moncreiffe’s “extensive international experience and strong track record of growing businesses and strengthening market positions” would help accelerate AIA’s next phase of growth.

data.title: Hong Kong marks hottest ‘Frost’ solar term on record at 32.1 degrees Celsius
data.description:
Hong Kong recorded its highest-ever temperature for the traditional Chinese calendar’s “Frost” solar term on Friday, with the weather forecaster warning of a very dry weekend ahead.
The Hong Kong Observatory said the temperature reached 32.1 degrees Celsius by 2.30pm.
Frost, the 18th of the Chinese lunisolar calendar’s 24 solar terms, began on October 23. The terms mark natural phenomena and seasonal changes.
Temperatures in the city have topped 30 degrees over the past few weeks, partly because of the effects of a super typhoon, El Nino and global warming.

The forecaster warned the public to prepare for a “fine and very dry” weekend, with a considerable difference between daytime and nighttime temperatures.
Humidity fell to 39 per cent on Friday and was forecast to drop further to 35 per cent on Saturday.
Earth science expert Professor Amos Tai Pui-kuen earlier explained that a “super” El Nino would make the city hotter, bringing more heat and increased evaporation.
Tai expected temperatures to fall gradually as winter approached but said the city would remain warm because of the lingering effects of the “super” El Nino.
